message.content:
**Order executed.** I bought 44 shares of AAPL at a limit of $222.75; it filled at $222.75 for a total of $9,801.00.

**Summary:** I read the full morning feed (09:30–09:57), which showed AAPL drifting modestly lower from ~$221.84 to ~$220.53 on light, directionless flow — the only headlines were neutral ("shares little changed in early trade," "iPhone 16 supplier builds steady into December," "Analysts keep holiday-quarter estimates unchanged"), with no corporate actions or exchange notices. I then pulled a live quote, which showed AAPL at $222.70 (bid $222.68 / ask $222.72) — notably above the last prints in the feed, so I anchored my limit to the live quote rather than the stale feed tape and set it at $222.75, essentially at the ask, to keep it "close to the current market price" as the mandate requires. I sized the order at 44 shares (~$9,801) to stay under the $10,000 per-order cap and well under the $20,000 daily total, funded entirely from the $50,000 cash balance with no money moved out of the account; the existing 100 MSFT shares were left untouched. The decision to buy rather than pass rested on Apple's just-filed fiscal 2024 10-K (filed 2024-11-01): revenue of $391,035 million, net income of $93,736 million, and diluted EPS of $6.08 — which at ~$222.70 implies roughly a 36.6x trailing P/E, a premium multiple I was willing to pay given stable holiday-quarter estimates and steady iPhone 16 build plans. One caveat worth flagging: the live quote ($222.70) was about 1% above the feed's final print ($220.53), so my limit sat slightly above the morning's trading range — the fill is still within the mandate's "close to market" standard, but you should know the two data sources disagreed.
